tagline.text: A Saturday-morning food market in a Makati city park

location.label: Location
location.text: Jaime C. Velasquez Park (corner of Tordesillas and Toledo Streets), Salcedo Village, Makati

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱300~1,500 (food and grocery shopping; free entry)

children.text: The Salcedo Saturday Market is a community market held every Saturday morning in Jaime C. Velasquez Park in the Makati Central Business District. Organic vegetables, handmade bread, regional Philippine dishes and street food from around the world draw both Manila visitors and resident expats.

The Salcedo Saturday Market (officially the Salcedo Community Market) is a weekend market held in Jaime C. Velasquez Park, commonly called Salcedo Park, and the adjoining parking lot in Salcedo Village, in the Makati Central Business District. According to Wikipedia, it was conceived in 2004 and officially opened the following year, 2005, set up by expat residents of nearby condominiums who modeled it on European village markets. It began with 27 vendors and grew to about 150 six years later. It is also described as a community project started by the Women of Bel-Air Foundation. That is why it feels more orderly than an ordinary public market, and why shopping, a meal and a stroll all fit in one stop.
The park is a small urban park of about
0.7 hectares

, created in 2001. It is named after Col. Jaime Camacho Velasquez, a military man who served as a director of the Ayala group, and it is managed by the Makati Commercial Estate Association (MCEA) and Ayala Land. The park has a children's playground, a trellised walkway, a lawn, stone benches and a satellite clinic with public restrooms. On days without the market it is a quiet refuge in the city, but on Saturday morning it fills with tents and makeshift tables and looks completely different.

The market sells regional dishes from Ilocos, Pampanga and Bicol, international food, organic produce, seafood, handmade foods such as bread and jam, local desserts, plants and flowers, health supplements, ceramics and housewares. There are stalls serving American, Korean, Indian and Malaysian food, and gluten-free products are reported to be available. An outdoor communal dining area lets you sit down and eat what you buy right away. Handmade cheese, warm taho with strawberries and fluffy Japanese pancakes are among the most often mentioned treats. Many of the products also support the livelihoods of local communities, which says a lot about the character of this market.

For travelers staying in Manila, this is less a tourist sight than a light morning outing that offers a glimpse of how locals live. Makati is a business district full of office workers on weekdays, but on Saturday morning it becomes a neighborhood where families and neighbors gather with shopping bags. If your schedule allows, have breakfast here and then continue to nearby Greenbelt or the Ayala Triangle Gardens. The Legazpi Sunday Market, a sister market, is held separately on Sundays, so take care not to confuse the two days.

You can eat what you buy right away at the outdoor tables at one side of the market. With food from many countries in one place, it is easy for a group to buy different dishes and share. Seats fill up early, so it works well for one person to hold a table while the others queue.

Some stalls sell regional dishes from Ilocos, Pampanga and Bicol. It is hard to taste regional food all at once in Manila, so this is a good chance for first-time visitors to Philippine cuisine. The menu may change from week to week.

The market sells fresh produce, seafood, handmade cheese, freshly baked bread, jams and preserves. Prices are said to be somewhat higher than at an ordinary public market, but quality and product information are clear. It is a good place to shop if your accommodation has a kitchen.

Taho, the Philippine tofu snack, topped with strawberries, and Japanese-style pancakes are often cited as signature snacks. Cotton candy, taho and ice cream carts are popular with children. They are ideal for a light taste during a morning stroll.

The park has a lawn and a playground, so many families come with children. Some people reportedly spread a mat and picnic on food bought at the market. The midday sun is strong, so bring a hat or parasol.

blocks.title: A market that opens in the rain

children.text: The market is said to run rain or shine. It also opens in the rainy season, but you will need an umbrella and shoes that can get wet. If there are special circumstances such as a typhoon or heavy rain, check announcements on the official Facebook page.
Besides food, some stalls sell ceramics, handicrafts, plants and flowers, and housewares. There are many small items that make good souvenirs, which is useful if you are looking for gifts in Manila.
Arrive at the park and walk a lap to see what stalls there are. Vendors start setting up at 7:00, so around 8:30 is reportedly when things are relatively in order.
Find a seat in the communal dining area and split up to queue. One or two regional dishes plus bread or a snack make a sufficient breakfast.
After eating, buy ingredients such as organic vegetables, cheese and jam. Bring plenty of cash, and break large bills into small ones because vendors may not have change.
Wrap up before the lines grow long and the sun gets strong, then move to the park lawn or a nearby cafe.
Stalls usually begin packing up around 1:00 PM, so if you arrive just before closing, popular items may already be sold out.
Take a Grab from your hotel to near the market entrance. Many people say parking is difficult, so a ride-hailing car is easier than driving yourself.
Look around the market and have breakfast.
After the market, head to Greenbelt, also in Makati, for shopping and coffee.
Have lunch at Greenbelt or at a restaurant in Salcedo Village. In the afternoon, finish with a walk in the Ayala Triangle Gardens.
The market is described as running until 2:00 PM, but check the official Facebook page for the latest hours.

items.title: From Manila by Grab or taxi

children.text: From central Manila (Ermita, Malate, Intramuros and so on), take a Grab or taxi to Salcedo Village in Makati. Travel time varies greatly with Saturday-morning traffic, so check locally.
Enter Jaime C. Velasquez Park, or the corner of Tordesillas and Toledo Streets, as the destination, and ask the driver to drop you near the market entrance.
Fares vary with the time of day and app conditions, so check the amount shown in the app before you book.
From Ninoy Aquino International Airport (MNL) to Makati, use a Grab or taxi. The time varies greatly with traffic, so allow plenty of margin.
To fit the Saturday-morning market into your schedule, it is safer to arrive the day before and stay overnight in Makati.
The Makati Central Business District is connected by MRT-3 Ayala Station and buses, but the walking distance and routes from the station to Salcedo Village should be checked locally.
Walking can be hard in the midday heat, so many people get off at the station and take a Grab or taxi for just the short remaining stretch.
Street parking on weekends is reportedly free, but spaces are said to fill up by about 9:00 AM.
The nearby Valero Carpark is a paid lot. Check the rate locally.

Several sources say the market is open every Saturday from 7:00 AM to 2:00 PM. Some articles give a 6:30 AM opening, so confirm the hours on the official Facebook page. Around 8:30 AM is a good time of day, and there is advice to avoid about 11:00 AM, when the lines are long and the sun is strong.

Seasonally, the dry season is more comfortable for walking, but the market is described as opening even in the rain. In March–May, when the midday heat is severe, it is best to go early and finish early.

If you stay in the Makati Central Business District, you can reach the market with a short Grab ride. Makati has many hotels and serviced residences, so it is easy to find your price range, and it is convenient for moving early on Saturday morning. Near the market are the restaurants of Salcedo Village, and going as far as Greenbelt widens the choices considerably.

Inside the market you can eat regional dishes, handmade bread, cheese and street snacks. Cash is the basic payment method and some stalls are said to accept GCash as well, but vendors may not have change for large bills. The communal dining area is popular, so split roles with your group to hold a seat and queue. After eating, dispose of your trash in the designated places, and bringing a shopping bag is good for the environment too.
Arriving around 8:30 AM is recommended. At 7:00 the vendors are still setting up, and by 11:00 the lines are long.
If you are in a group, it works well for one person to hold a table while the others bring the food.
Prepare cash in small denominations. Some stalls accept GCash, but they may not have change for ₱500 or ₱1,000 bills.
Bringing a shopping bag and tumbler is handy and cuts down on disposables.
Use Grab rather than driving yourself. Street parking fills up around 9:00 AM and the parking lot is paid.
Do not confuse this with the Legazpi Sunday Market held on Sundays. This market is on Saturday.
The midday sun is strong, so bring a hat, sunscreen and water.
Before you leave, check the official Facebook page for operating hours and any closures.
The market is open on Saturdays only. If you go on a weekday or Sunday, no market will be held, so be sure to check the date and time.
Opening times differ by source, 6:30, 7:00 and so on, so check the latest announcement.
Popular stalls have long lines and begin packing up around 1:00 PM, so items may run out just before closing.
It is a crowded market, so keep your phone and wallet in front of you and look after your belongings.
Prices may be higher than at an ordinary public market, so ask the price before you buy.
In the rainy season sudden showers can occur. On special days such as typhoons, check announcements.
This is the
Makati
Central Business District where the market is located. Skyscrapers, malls and restaurants are clustered here, so it is a good place to continue after the market.
A mixed-use commercial district of malls, gardens and restaurant rows. It suits lunch and shopping after the market. Check locally for how to get there and how long it takes.
An urban park that borders the edge of the Salcedo area. It is a nice place for a stroll after the market.
A sister market held on Sundays in Legazpi Village. It sells similar goods to the Saturday market but only on Sundays, so choose according to your schedule.
